vignette:
He is forty-five now, a European journalist with a practiced way of speaking that sounds calm even when his hands give him away. In session, he sits upright, one ankle crossed over the other, fingertips worrying the seam of his notebook. He has spent most of his adult life moving toward danger with a press badge around his neck, telling himself that bearing witness is a kind of service. For years he had worked in conflict zones and authoritarian states, filing clean, controlled pieces under deadline, then coming home to his wife with gifts from airport kiosks and stories edited down to something almost entertaining. He had always believed that fear could be managed if it was named quickly enough.

Three years ago, while reporting on political detentions in a remote region, that belief gives way. He is traveling with a local driver and fixer when their vehicle is stopped at an improvised checkpoint. Men with covered faces pull him out, take his phone, bind his wrists, and push him into the back of another truck. What follows is fragmented in the way he tells it: diesel fumes, gravel under his cheek, the pressure of a boot between his shoulder blades. He remembers trying, at first, to explain who he is in the careful, diplomatic tone he uses with officials. Then the tone falls away. In captivity, time loses structure. He is kept in a small room with no window, interrogated, threatened, struck often enough that he stops predicting when the next blow will come. Sometimes there is shouting just outside the door. Sometimes there is nothing for hours except the scrape of a bowl on the floor and the sound of his own breathing, too loud in the dark.

What stays with him most is not only the fear that he will die there, but the humiliating helplessness of waiting for other people to decide whether he is fed, mocked, beaten, or ignored. He begins to track tiny details to stay oriented: the number of steps from the wall to the door, the different coughs of the guards, the moment in the day when sunlight briefly appears under the frame. He tells himself stories in his head in complete journalistic sentences, as if turning his experience into copy might stop it from swallowing him. On some nights he hears another prisoner crying. On others he thinks he hears his wife's voice and knows, even then, that it cannot be real.

He is eventually released through negotiations he still does not fully understand. The reunion at home is photographed, and he smiles in every picture with a face that looks to him like someone else's. At first he tries to perform gratitude. Friends bring food. Colleagues call him courageous. He says he is lucky. He says he is recovering. But ordinary domestic life begins to feel unreal and strangely unsafe. In bed, he wakes drenched in sweat, convinced for several seconds that he is back in the cell and cannot move his hands. If his wife touches him unexpectedly in sleep, he jerks away before he recognizes her. He starts checking locks repeatedly each night, then checking the windows, then standing in the hallway listening for footsteps that never come.

During the day, sounds seize him before thought catches up: a slammed car door, boots on the stairs, a low male voice outside a café. He avoids small interior rooms and becomes agitated in elevators. He cannot bear having the bathroom door fully closed. When he tries to return to reporting, he finds himself scanning every room for exits instead of listening to interviews. A source pauses too long before answering, and his heart begins to pound as if he is again being watched for the wrong response. He misses deadlines, something he had almost never done. He opens transcripts and finds his mind snagging on words like detained, transferred, extraction. Sometimes he stares at a blinking cursor for an hour.

His wife tells him he is home, but home has narrowed around his fear. He sits with his back to the wall in restaurants. He declines invitations from friends because the effort of appearing normal exhausts him. He drinks more than he means to in the evenings, hoping to mute the images that arrive unbidden: the bucket in the corner of the cell, the crack in the concrete, the guard tapping something metallic against the door. Shame threads through much of what he says. He is ashamed that he survived by complying. Ashamed that part of him still imagines he should have taken notes, remembered names, made use of what happened. Ashamed that his wife has learned to announce herself softly when entering a room.

What disturbs him nearly as much as the memories is the person he has become in relation to them. He used to be curious, improvisational, drawn to uncertainty. Now he is rigid with planning and still unconvinced he can keep danger out. He no longer reads accounts of hostage situations, yet he compulsively searches the news for updates from the region where he was held. He says he wants to know the truth, but he can feel his body tightening even as he clicks. Some part of him remains in that room, listening for footsteps, trying to infer from the smallest sound whether the next moment will bring pain. Even now, sitting in a safe office on a quiet afternoon, he notices the position of the door before he says anything else.
